title: High school bands and intensive practice in San Francisco
summary: In school orchestras and a noon-hour dance band, with a strict father who allowed only church music, he practised melodic playing for hours; he recalls bandmate Phil Lambert.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Picking up the horn: first instrument and the trombone

blocks.x: much music, I couldn't -- I didn't keep track of dates too well. I just knew that I wasn't -- I was in grammar school into high school, and by this time I had gotten so I could play in the grammar school orchestra on trombone and the high school orches- tras on trombone, and of course my father was a very, very strict person, and it was all right for me to play melodies and church pieces and in the choir, finally, on trombone, but no jazz or no dance -- whatever you call the dance type music at that -- in that era.
Did you think that was what you wanted to play?

Well, I wanted to play all of them. Our family had a feeling, it seemed, for music, and we could acquire a capability of playing any type of music. I tried everything from symphony to concert to jazz, all those music. It seemed very easy for me to acquire the feeling, and so by the time I was into high school, I was playing all of these different types of music fairly well. Of course, I was continually in the school bands, the school orchestras, and I had even gotten so I could play in the school dance band, which used to give per- formances at noon hour. During the noon hour we'd go up in the gym, and they would have school dances during the noon hour.
Now, by this time I'm over in San Francisco, and I remember one of the associates in our dance orchestra very well. His name was -- his name was Phil Lambert, and later -- many

years later I ran into Phil Lambert, and he was the director of the pit orchestra at the Fox Theater in Washington, D. C., and he told me he was going from there into New York into some orchestra, but I never saw him any more. But by this time I was thoroughly interested, and trombone was my instrument.

From this time on began my very intensive study of trombone and of the music that I would like to play on it. As I said before, I could never get the idea out of my head that if a cello, who was a sort of a slide instrument also, or a violin, could play melodies, why couldn't a trombone, which was a slide type instrument. They couldn't play melodies instead of the usual oompah or whatever, dixie type playing that was done on it. And so, therefore, I would rehearse for hours and hours, playing melodies, listening to tone and trying to improve my conception of how I wanted the instrument to sound. I would sit up after school and way up in the night with no lights on and just listen to the tones come back from the walls and phrase things as I would like to hear them, until I became quite adept at the playing of these melodies, plus the regular score type trombone in school orchestras, and by now music was my primary interest.
